newsitem.title: PERU: Peru crisis negotiator - puppet or power-broker?.
newsitem.headline: Peru crisis negotiator - puppet or power-broker?.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori's surprising appointment of Education Minister Domingo Palermo as chief government negotiator in Peru's hostage crisis thrust the low-profile official into the international limelight.
But the appointment split opinion in Peru over whether it was a subtle masterstroke or a grave miscalculation.

"He's a gray minister," Javier Diez Canseco, an opposition congressman and former hostage, said. "With the choice of Palermo as the government's negotiator Fujimori is trying to show that he is not giving this crisis much importance."
Palermo, who entered politics in 1995 as one of the Lima mayor's team of advisers, was a surprise choice as education minister when Fujimori reshuffled his cabinet last April.

Despite his key role, he has entered the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence just once in the 23 days since about 20 heavily armed guerrillas stormed a cocktail party and took hundreds of VIP guests hostage.

That first face-to-face meeting with the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas saw the release of 20 hostages and created optimism that the siege would end quickly and peacefully. But that was 12 days ago and talks seem to have been broken off indefinitely with 74 hostages still held.

The apparent lack of progress has led to calls for Palermo to be replaced by a higher profile international mediator such as former U.S. President Jimmy Carter, Pope John Paul II or even Cuban leader Fidel Castro.

"The choice (of Palermo) as just a messenger does not follow any strategy to end the crisis. The government wants to demonstrate its authoritarianism and that it will not give in to the MRTA's demands," political analyst Pedro Planas said.

Fujimori has refused to negotiate directly with the rebels and flatly rejected their main demand that he pardon some 400 jailed comrades. By selecting a minister with a portfolio unrelated to the rebels' demands, Fujimori underscored his "no concessions" approach to the crisis, analysts said.

But those close to Palermo insist that his nomination as the government's chief negotiator has more to do with his personal skills than a deliberate ploy by Fujimori. A civil engineer by training, Palermo, 50, is a quiet man and devoted to the arts, particularly classical music.

"He is a very intelligent man, a problem solver," Augusto Ferrero, a lawyer and close personal friend of the education minister, said. "Never in all the time that I have known him have I seen him be abrupt, he never loses his cool, he is thoughtful and always analyses everything."
Despite his somewhat ill-defined role in bringing an end to the siege, many still feel that Palermo's nomination will eventually be seen as a stroke of genius by Fujimori.

"The dificult mission which the government has given him is definitely suited to his character. He is very patient, a very efficient and low-profile person," Marta Mifflin, director of local radio station Sol y Armonia, said.
